newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen says doors open on human rights.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen says doors open on human rights.

text.p: Cambodian leader Hun Sen said the state of human rights in the country was "very good" and he had ordered his government to give unrestricted access to rights groups to investigate reports of abuses.
He said he had instructed the ministries of interior, defence and justice to open their doors freely to the Red Cross and human rights investigators.
"Very good," Hun Sen told reporters when asked about the state of human rights in Cambodia.
"I allow Red Cross and human rights (workers); if they come anywhere, they can see, they can go, I allow," he said.

U.N. human rights workers estimate 40 people were killed after Hun Sen ousted his senior co-premier, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, on July 6. Most of the victims were believed to have been the prince's supporters, including several senior military officials and their bodyguards.
Hun Sen criticised a U.N. rights office on the weekend, saying it had frightened people into fleeing the country.

In the immediate aftermath of Ranariddh's overthrow, government officials said one senior royalist official was executed after he was taken into custody and at least one other was killed in fighting. But the government denied human rights abuses.
The U.N. Centre for Human Rights in Cambodia has unearthed the bodies of three executed men in past weeks, all believed to have been royalist supporters.
The U.N. office also found evidence that captured royalist soldiers had been tortured while in custody of government forces under Hun Sen.
Scores of royalist politicians and supporters fled Cambodia after Hun Sen's coup, including some 20 members of parliament.
Hun Sen on Monday appealed to opposition politicians to return to Phnom Penh saying their safety would be guaranteed.
The Khmer Rouge guerrilla group said on Monday Hun Sen should be brought before an international court for the alleged killing of Ranariddh's supporters.
"The puppet Hun Sen has to be sent to the international court and sentenced in accordance with his criminal act," guerrilla radio said in a broadcast monitored in Phnom Penh.
The guerrillas' clandestine radio has long been their main propaganda mouthpiece.

More than a million Cambodians were killed during the Khmer Rouge's 1975-79 "killing fields" rule. Rebel leader Pol Pot was sentenced to life under house arrest by his former comrades at their jungle court show trial on July 25.
Hun Sen said Pol Pot should be brought before an international tribunal to answer for his crimes.
